title: Concept Convergence
summary: Concept Convergence follows exploration by comparing locally strong solutions against the coherence of the whole system. It may identify a Creative Navy-described competitive vector when tensions reveal deeper market, user and organisational forces, but it can also operate as prioritisation when the option space contains no local-versus-system tension.
keyFacts: Concept Convergence addresses the conflict between what works best for individual challenges and what works best for the system as a whole.
The process first identifies the strongest isolated solution for each challenge, then evaluates which combination creates the most coherent system.
The method phase produces a product concept, documented tensions and trade-offs, rationale for the chosen configuration, and shared stakeholder understanding of what is being built and why.

A Creative Navy-described competitive vector can be identified when the tension reveals alignment between market forces, user needs and organisational capability, but the method phase does not automatically produce one.
Structuring frameworks can be Concept Convergence artefacts when a process has structural properties that govern later design decisions.

In the Squaremind case, the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework preceded screen design and was tested through an ecological study with 29 users, 27 independent completions and 12 of 12 recoveries among users who got stuck.
Concept Convergence can include design education when stakeholders receive context-specific user behaviour reasoning alongside design options.
Constraint respecting can operate through Concept Convergence when client requirements, technical constraints and user needs eliminate options from the viable option space.
In the Raymarine case, the selected fixed-role control model accepted a median target browsing time penalty of 2.30 seconds compared with the contextual model under prototype test conditions.
Concept Convergence duration varies from 1–2 weeks for straightforward systems to 4–6 weeks when many stakeholders need alignment.

bodySections.heading: Concept Convergence in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Concept Convergence is the method phase that makes tensions between local optimisation and system coherence explicit, examines what drives those tensions, and converges on a product concept, structuring framework or prioritised configuration.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats this tension as evidence. The work first determines which solution performs best in isolation for each challenge. It then assesses which combination of solutions creates the most coherent system, which trade-offs that configuration introduces, and which forces make the conflict appear.

bodySections.heading: Concept Convergence Makes Local-Versus-System Tension Explicit
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Concept Convergence starts by identifying local optimisation. A workflow may be clearest for one role while creating blind spots for another role. A layout may work for simple cases while making complex cases illegible. A pattern may feel intuitive in one module while behaving differently in another.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method documents these tensions explicitly so that stakeholders can see which trade-offs are real constraints, which alternatives were rejected, and why the chosen configuration is more coherent than the isolated winners.

The next step is tension-driven reasoning. Creative Navy examines what drives the conflict itself: why the locally strong option conflicts with the systemic option. The source of the tension may reveal shifts in how the market operates, unresolved strategic questions, or misalignment between a business model and user reality.

bodySections.heading: Concept Convergence Can Identify a Creative Navy-Described Competitive Vector
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A Creative Navy-described competitive vector is the direction where market forces, user needs and organisational capability align to create defensible advantage. Concept Convergence is where this direction can be identified when the option space contains a genuine tension between local and system-level optimisation.

The method phase does not treat tension as a problem to remove. The tension can indicate where the product needs to evolve, where competitors may struggle, and where strategic decisions will matter most. The resulting concept explains what the solution is, why the configuration works better than alternatives explored, and how it positions the product as the forces driving the tension continue to evolve.

Concept Convergence is not compromise. It is conscious navigation of real constraints toward a configuration that preserves differentiation while resolving complexity. Competitors who optimise only locally can end up with feature sets that do not cohere.

bodySections.heading: Concept Convergence Produces a Concept, Trade-Off Record and Rationale
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Concept Convergence produces a product concept that shows the chosen configuration. It also produces explicit documentation of tensions and trade-offs, a rationale for why the chosen approach beats alternatives, and a shared understanding across stakeholders about what is being built and why.

The output can take different forms. In some engagements, the output is a concept brief that describes the chosen direction. In other engagements, the output is a structuring framework that expresses the causal architecture of the experience. Where a process has structural properties that govern all later design decisions, a diagram or explicit artefact can be the correct convergence output.

Concept Convergence commonly lasts 1–2 weeks for straightforward systems. When many stakeholders need alignment, the method phase can take 4–6 weeks.

bodySections.heading: Structuring Frameworks Can Be Concept Convergence Artefacts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A structuring framework is appropriate when the process being designed has structural properties that determine how subsequent design decisions must behave. In Concept Convergence, the structuring framework makes explicit the logic that later design decisions must satisfy, rather than leaving that logic to be reconstructed from individual screens.

This output is distinct from a design system and from a concept brief. A design system documents components and rules. A concept brief describes a chosen direction. A structuring framework expresses the causal architecture of the experience.

The Squaremind dermatology scanning device case shows this use of Concept Convergence. The engagement required an embedded patient interface for a full-body dermatology scanner operated without clinical supervision. The convergence challenge was structural: every design decision across positioning screens, progress indicators, arm-raise instructions, error states and recovery prompts had to satisfy the same underlying logic.

Creative Navy introduced the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework during Concept Convergence and delivered it as a diagram mapping all three layers across every step of the flow, including recursive correction paths. The artefact preceded screen design. It was the architecture that screen design had to satisfy, not a description of screens already produced.

The following Creative Navy-recorded iteration counts were then worked through against that architecture: full scan process, 5 iterations; progress bar, 5 iterations; progressive disclosure elements, 5 iterations; pause button, 7 iterations; body selection, 3 iterations; patient ID, 2 iterations.

Post-redesign ecological testing with 29 users produced 27 independent completions and 12 of 12 recoveries among users who got stuck. This is case evidence that the convergence architecture held under real conditions in that test context.

bodySections.heading: Design Education Can Accelerate Concept Convergence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method can use design education as a convergence mechanism when the client team is closely involved in design reviews. In this use, each design direction is presented with an explanation of the user behaviour patterns it addresses. Stakeholders receive not only what the design does, but why users behave in ways that make the design necessary.

In the Squaremind engagement, each design presentation included design education content about users and user behaviour. The review process therefore became a shared understanding of the problem, rather than a choice between options that the client could only evaluate aesthetically.

The CDR Foodlab engagement is a second documented instance in a materially different context. CDR Foodlab involved multiple stakeholders reviewing iterative design directions for a constrained embedded instrument with non-specialist users. Every design presentation was accompanied by rationale documents and verbal briefing explaining the specific user behaviours that made each design decision necessary. The content was developed directly from 13 user interviews and the workaround catalogue.

The Enhesa engagement is a third documented instance in an enterprise SaaS context. It involved three named client-side stakeholders reviewing iterative design directions for a web-based legal compliance platform. Design education was promised at engagement start and delivered as a standing element of every presentation. The Enhesa content was grounded in 95 session recordings, a 31-workaround catalogue across four categories, and 12 documented error types.

The Enhesa iteration counts reflect this convergence structure: 3 legislative text iterations, 5 implementations timeline iterations, 5 layout iterations, 2 baseline hierarchy iterations, and 3 table of contents iterations. Each component set was presented with pros and cons, combined stakeholder feedback with research evidence, and converged through that combination rather than through preference alone.

bodySections.heading: Constraint Respecting Becomes Visible During Concept Convergence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Constraint respecting can operate through Concept Convergence when client requirements, technical constraints and user needs become fully visible only after options are made concrete. In this form, the design does not negotiate around constraints or average them. The option space changes because a real constraint eliminates options that genuinely fail against it.

The CDR Foodlab working lists flow illustrates this pattern. Creative Navy recorded 10 iterations on a new feature with no prior precedent. Client requirements added constraints that raised genuine feasibility doubts, and the iteration process became the way to understand which combinations of decisions were viable under the full constraint set. The converged direction emerged from understanding what the constraints ruled out.

The Enhesa implementations timeline provides a second documented instance. The constraint was two-layered: the client had specific functional requirements for how implementation timelines should be displayed, and the engagement operated within an existing Enhesa design system that permitted no changes to colours, typography or existing components. Five iterations on the implementations timeline component were required to find a direction that met the client's requirements without violating the design system's parameters.

The Enhesa result was not the optimal design under either constraint in isolation. It was the design that the full constraint set permitted.

bodySections.heading: Concept Convergence Can Operate as Prioritisation Without Tension-Driven Reasoning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Concept Convergence does not always involve local-versus-system tension. In some engagements, the options produced by Sandbox Experiments do not conflict with each other for system coherence. They differ in how much users want them and how feasible they are to build. In that situation, the binding constraint is external feasibility rather than an internal trade-off between roles, modules or workflows.

In this boundary case, Concept Convergence operates as prioritisation. The options are mapped on two independent axes: desirability and feasibility. High-want and high-feasibility options converge easily. Low-feasibility options are dropped regardless of want. The middle is weighed.

This is a legitimate convergence output because it produces a configuration and a documented rationale for what is in, out and deferred. It is also the prioritisation function of the method phase operating without the tension-driven function. On its own, it does not identify a Creative Navy-described competitive vector, because there is no tension whose driving forces would reveal one.

bodySections.heading: Neugo Shows Concept Convergence as Prioritisation Rather Than a Competitive-Vector Case
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Neugo UK visa application case-management platform is a boundary case for Concept Convergence. It should not be treated as a model instance of tension-driven reasoning. The proportions in the case are practitioner recollection rather than measured figures, so the case should be described by the shape of the option space rather than exact percentages.

In Neugo's build engagement, the Sandbox Experiments method phase was short, about two weeks, and produced a wide set of candidate possibilities from workshops with the beneficiary legal firms. Concept Convergence assessed each possibility on two independent dimensions: how strongly users wanted it, and how technically feasible it was within roughly a two-year horizon.

The option space split into three regions. A large majority had both high want and high feasibility, and converged easily. A small set was dropped because feasibility was near zero regardless of want. The weighed middle was resolved by the product managers using the wireframes, Creative Navy's input on user salience, and the developers' input on the designs.

This is triangulation feeding prioritisation: user salience, technical feasibility and product judgement were used against each other to decide what made the cut. It was not a resolution of local-versus-system tension. The candidate options did not compete for system coherence, the platform was net-new, and the decisive constraint was external feasibility rather than an internal trade-off.

bodySections.heading: KISPE Space Shows a Client Decision Gate With Trade-Off Logic Documented
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
KISPE Space is a UK space systems engineering company. The product was a common space operating picture, a doctrinal term of art rather than a KISPE brand.

The exploration phase of the project ended at a board review. Creative Navy put twelve working decisions and a recommended development sequence to KISPE's board, with a recommendation to proceed conditionally. The board endorsed the product architecture as the working direction, approved a staged scope with explicit decision gates for the uncertain features, and authorised the seven-sprint UX development phase.

This engagement record is not user validation. It is not an outcome claim. The twelve decisions were not approved requirements. The endorsement authorised detailed design against a direction while retaining the right to modify or reject individual solutions after validation.

The KISPE Space architecture adopted a hybrid model over two credible alternatives that were built and assessed. A permanently dominant map kept geographic continuity but squeezed catalogue work, metadata and preview into competing panel space. Fully separate modules gave specialist tools room but allowed the area of interest to change unnoticed between modules. The hybrid kept a small, explicit shared context: confirmed area, temporal perspective and return path, while giving each task workspace its own layout.

The accepted costs were recorded. Shared state is more complex. Local filters must not be mistaken for global ones. A persistent header costs real pixels on a compact device.

bodySections.heading: KISPE Space Decisions Show Concept Convergence Through Explicit Trade-Offs
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used Concept Convergence in the KISPE Space work to make interaction contracts explicit. A confirmed area of interest was separated from the map viewport. Panning or zooming changed what was visible but did not change what was being queried. The visible extent as implicit query boundary was rejected because a minor pan could silently change the meaning of every result returned. The accepted costs were an extra confirmation, area management and the difficulty of editing a polygon on touch hardware.

Query lineage was specified as an interaction contract. Every area-scoped request carried the area identity, geometry signature, filter set, temporal perspective and generation time. A late response from a superseded request could not populate the current results. The accepted cost was request lineage and cancellation semantics, not only a loading spinner.

The selected object and selected area were independent states. Inspecting a map object did not move the area of interest to that object's footprint. Hiding a layer did not silently redefine the area. When a selected object was filtered out of view, the interface indicated that state.

Other trade-off decisions included grouped selection lists for overlapping map symbols, return navigation that restored the prior viewport and confirmed area without implying a fresh fetch, and three temporal perspectives that framed the view without rewriting a record's own time. The sharpest recorded self-criticism was that Current could still be misread as live, so per-record stamps and explicit labelling remained essential.

The KISPE Space product was built. Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs, so the case supports designed decisions but not a verified design-fidelity claim.

bodySections.heading: Maritime VTS Work Shows Tensions Resolved Rather Than Averaged
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The maritime case involved a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. A formal gate was a condition of the engagement from the proposal onwards. The gate was chaired by the programme sponsor with product, engineering and commercial owners present, and Creative Navy presenting.

Three decision options were defined in advance: proceed, revise the reference product or scope, or stop and retain the discovery package as a self-contained strategic deliverable. The reference product was selected on five weighted criteria: commercial significance at 25%, system transfer value at 25%, access to representative users at 20%, high-consequence UX learning at 15%, and implementation feasibility at 15%.

Five candidates were scored out of 100. VTS scored 90, inland vessel tracking 77, voice communications 71, electronic reporting 67, and lock planning 63. VTS was selected because it combined geographic surveillance, uncertain sensor observations, differentiated alerts, event history, incident state, equipment health and shift handover in one environment. Voice communications scored highly on consequence and lost on portability, because hardware-coupled control semantics limited general reuse.

Six objections were recorded and dispositioned rather than resolved offline. They covered whether one redesigned application would persuade in multi-product tenders, whether a design file would translate into multiple frontend stacks, whether ordinary toggles could carry radio transmission and resource selection, the risk of changing familiar controls without operator validation, financial protection against expansion into nine full redesigns, and representation of administrative and planning applications.

The recommendation changed the shape of the work. Instead of a common modern interface across nine products, the documented direction was one application developed to full depth as a reference, a technology-neutral semantic design system built in parallel, bounded transfer tests in four other products, and implementation contracts and governance handed to the client's engineers. Nine products were audited; one was designed to full depth.

bodySections.heading: Maritime VTS Architecture Decisions Show Specialised Behaviour Winning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used Concept Convergence in the maritime VTS work to resolve tensions at architecture level. Three multidisciplinary disagreements were resolved in review and recorded: panel mobility against target visibility, one alert inbox against operational meaning, and visual certainty against defensible provenance. In all three, the specialised behaviour won.

A dashboard landing view was built and rejected. It was attractive for commercial presentations because it exposed many functions at once, but it moved the active traffic picture into a secondary container and forced operators to reacquire sector, object and layer context after every inspection. A map-as-bounded-card variant was rejected with it.

The dockable inspector was chosen over two alternatives that each had a real advantage. An unrestricted floating inspector preserved maximum map width when closed and could obscure the selected symbol in dense traffic. A permanently open side panel removed arbitrary occlusion and consumed map width even with no investigation active. The selected contextual dock opened on a predictable edge, followed the selected evidence reference rather than a screen coordinate, collapsed without clearing selection, and could move to a permitted secondary display. The always-open panel was retained as a documented installation option.

Vessel, track and observation were kept as three separate objects. A single resolved vessel record was rejected because it obscured what the system actually knew. The selected model kept a vessel identity record, a tracked object with an association status, and timestamped observations each carrying their own source. Association could be resolved, unresolved, changed or unknown.

A numeric association-confidence badge was explored and refused. It would have compressed uncertainty into one familiar control, but the client's engineering could not supply a calibrated, operationally defensible confidence figure. The interface therefore stated the association as unresolved, and the specification recorded that the interface does not synthesise an association confidence score, a source time or an authorisation decision. Missing values appeared as unknown or not available. This was a data-provenance decision, not an AI treatment; the engagement had no model, performed no inference and made no recommendations.

The maritime design system reached production. No design-fidelity comparison is recorded, so the evidence does not support a claim that the design shipped as designed. Control-room references are limited to operational VTS control rooms at a customer site.

bodySections.heading: Schone Airspace Group Shows Consolidation Into One Interaction Architecture
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Schone Airspace Group used Concept Convergence after a consultative and scope-setting exploration phase of the project. Detailed UX and UI scope was confirmed at the conclusion of exploration, not before it. The client was asked to decide what to commission after seeing the analysis.

Creative Navy recorded six cross-system design principles at the end of exploration, each with a practical implication: keep the aircraft identifiable; distinguish intent from observed state; keep critical information stable; make uncertainty visible; match controls to available capability; support work across interruptions.

Four operational scenarios were used to test the exploration direction in combination rather than in isolation: planning a survey over uneven ground; switching from flight monitoring to visual inspection; a warning concerning another connected aircraft; reviewing a mission that ended early.

These are engagement records, not operational outcomes. The mission control product was built and is in test. The evidence does not support a deployment claim, operational-use claim, flight-safety claim, airworthiness claim or certification credential.

bodySections.heading: Raymarine Shows Control-Model Selection With a Recorded Cost
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Raymarine provides a documented example of Concept Convergence resolving a system-level control ambiguity before high-fidelity design. Four control models were compared against the same operational scenarios for a next-generation fixed-mount VHF in the Ray53, Ray63 and Ray73 fixed-mount VHF line context.

Model A used a contextual rotary control. The encoder adjusted channel on the radio view, target on the AIS view and selection in menus. It was fast and reused hardware efficiently, but carried a risk of hidden mode changes and error after interruptions.

Model B used a fixed role. The channel encoder always changed channel, while directional keys and softkeys managed contextual interaction. It was predictable, learnable and stable for communication behaviour, but some AIS tasks required additional key presses.

Model C used an explicit mode. The encoder changed purpose only after a deliberate press or other mode switch. It supported powerful navigation with a visible contract, but the operator still had to track an extra state under pressure. Model C was examined in two variants and both were rejected. Persisting mode preserved local task continuity but created a memory burden after attention shifted. Resetting mode made channel tuning predictable after interruptions but changed the meaning of the next rotary movement unexpectedly.

Model D used a dedicated new control. An additional input dedicated to secondary navigation or target selection would have offered high speed without overloading the channel control, but it introduced hardware, enclosure and feasibility implications. Model D was set aside rather than rejected on merit. It remained an industrial design option if later product testing identified unacceptable AIS browsing effort.

bodySections.heading: Raymarine Fixed-Role Control Accepted Slower Browsing to Remove Ambiguity
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method selected the fixed-role model in the Raymarine work because consistency outweighed isolated task speed. One or two extra key presses were preferable to uncertainty about whether an input changed the tuned channel. Incoming calls or alerts did not silently change the meaning of the rotary encoder. Priority channel access, distress initiation and push-to-talk did not depend on what the display currently showed. Hardware changes remained optional.

The retained trade-off was recorded at the moment of decision. Directional navigation through dense traffic needed usability checks, and the subsequent sprint was tasked with testing whether filtering, list sorting or accelerated key navigation would reduce selection effort.

The risk was characterised as structural rather than cosmetic. If the same encoder silently changed purpose, adding labels later could not fully remove the ambiguity. Resolving the ambiguity before high-fidelity design protected the subsequent flow work from rework.

The recorded comparison included the selected model's cost. Median target browsing time was 6.25 seconds for the contextual model and 8.55 seconds for the fixed-role model, a 2.30 second penalty under the selected model. Creative Navy designed the test protocols, moderated all twenty-four sessions and analysed the results. Raymarine supplied the physical bench mockup on which the sessions ran. Eighteen people took part across the twenty-four sessions.

These findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture. They are not a measure of radio performance, real-world calling accuracy or outcomes at sea. The radio was built and released, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded. The case evidence also does not claim measured error reduction or engineering cost saving at the time of the pivot.

bodySections.heading: Concept Convergence Prevents Design Systems From Freezing Temporary Compromises
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method connects Concept Convergence to design system work. Without examining what drives conflicts, design systems can become traps: patterns that crystallise one moment's compromise and prevent teams from responding as context shifts.

When the forces creating tensions are understood, a design system can remain responsive. The design system can document not only components and rules, but the reasoning behind them: which decisions protect the Creative Navy-described competitive vector, which constraints are temporary, where flexibility must be preserved, and how patterns should evolve.

strongClaims: Concept Convergence resolves the tension between local optimisation and system coherence by comparing isolated best solutions with coherent system configurations.
Concept Convergence can identify a Creative Navy-described competitive vector when local-versus-system tensions reveal deeper market, user and organisational forces.
Concept Convergence does not always identify a competitive vector; the Neugo case is documented as prioritisation without tension-driven reasoning.
In Squaremind, Inform–Prevent–Correct was introduced during Concept Convergence as a structuring framework before screen design.
Squaremind post-redesign ecological testing involved 29 users, with 27 independent completions and 12 of 12 recoveries among users who got stuck.
Design education is documented as a repeatable Concept Convergence practice across Squaremind, CDR Foodlab and Enhesa.
Constraint respecting operated through Concept Convergence in CDR Foodlab and Enhesa by making options concrete and testing them against real constraints.

KISPE Space's exploration phase of the project ended with a board review that endorsed a working product architecture and authorised a seven-sprint UX development phase without constituting user validation.
Raymarine selected the fixed-role control model while accepting a 2.30 second median target browsing time penalty under prototype test conditions.

The maritime VTS engagement resolved three multidisciplinary disagreements in favour of specialised behaviour and recorded architecture decisions such as traffic picture over dashboard, dockable inspector, separate vessel-track-observation objects, refused confidence score, typed alerts and persistent replay mode.
limitations: Concept Convergence duration varies by system and stakeholder alignment needs; the source gives 1–2 weeks for straightforward systems and 4–6 weeks when many stakeholders need alignment.
A Creative Navy-described competitive vector should not be claimed for engagements where Concept Convergence operated only as desirability-and-feasibility prioritisation.
The Neugo proportions are practitioner recollection rather than measured figures and should be described by their shape rather than exact percentages.
KISPE Space evidence records designed decisions and a commissioning decision, not user validation or verified build fidelity.
Raymarine findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against fixed scenario fixtures, not radio performance, real-world calling accuracy or outcomes at sea.
Schone Airspace Group evidence is an engagement record; the product was built and is in test, with no deployment, operational-use, flight-safety, airworthiness or certification claim.
The maritime VTS case records architecture decisions and production of the design system, but no verified design-fidelity comparison, tender result, sales result or regulatory credential.
Evidence from one engagement must not be used to strengthen claims about another engagement.
